Knowledge-Based Authentication Methods Knowledge-based methods rely on ' something you know '. These are often the most familiar — but also the most vulnerable. Illustration of a password entry screen with the text 'Enter password' and a masked input field showing six asterisks. Passwords User-defined secret strings that must be remembered • Prone to phishing attacks • Often reused across sites • Strengthen with password managers Illustration of a hand holding a smartphone displaying a PIN entry screen with the text 'Enter your pin' and a numeric keypad. PIN Codes Typically short numeric sequences for device unlock • Vulnerable to shoulder surfing • Limited complexity (usually 4-6 digits) • Common in ATMs and mobile devices Illustration of a smartphone screen displaying a security question prompt: 'Let's get you back in', 'What is your answer?', and 'Enter your verification'. Security Questions Answers to predefined personal questions • Can be researched via social media • Often have guessable answers • Commonly used for account recovery Illustration of a blue and purple ribbon forming a loop with the text 'SECURE CONNECTION' overlaid. Passphrases Longer, more complex sequences of words • Typically more secure than passwords • Easier to remember than complex passwords • Best used as part of MFA, not alone ⚠ Remember: All knowledge-based methods benefit from length and complexity but should ideally be used as part of Multi-Factor Authentication rather than alone.

Case Study: RockYou2021 – Password Reuse Breach 1 Event In 2021, the largest known password leak occurred — called RockYou2021. 2 What Happened • Over 8 billion passwords were posted online in a mega leak. • Data was compiled from years of breaches (e.g., LinkedIn, Adobe). • Attackers used these for credential stuffing: trying passwords across many sites. 3 Why This Is a Knowledge-Based Failure Passwords = 'something you know' (knowledge factor). People reused the same passwords across services. No second factor (MFA) meant easy unauthorized access. 4 Lesson Passwords are easily leaked, guessed, or reused. Never rely on knowledge factors alone for secure authentication.

Case Study: Coinbase Breach via SIM-Swap (2022) A simple line-art icon of a calendar with a date marker. Calendar icon Event In 2022, attackers exploited SMS-based MFA to access Coinbase accounts. A simple line-art icon of two stylized human figures. People icon What Happened: Attackers used social engineering to perform a SIM-swap with the victim's mobile provider. They gained control of the victim's phone number and intercepted SMS OTP codes. With previously leaked passwords and the intercepted OTP, they accessed accounts. A simple line-art icon of a clock face with an arrow indicating a cycle. Clock icon Why It Mattered: Showed SMS OTP can be phished or hijacked via telecom weaknesses. A simple line-art icon of a checkmark inside a circle. Checkmark icon Outcome: Coinbase strengthened MFA practices and advised users to use app-based TOTP or FIDO2.

Behavioral Biometrics Analyzes typing rhythm, gait, or mouse movements ✅ Continuous authentication without user action ⚠️ Challenges with Biometric Authentication: May require special hardware - Privacy concerns with storage - Risk of biometric spoofing 💡 Best used as part of MFA or with local secure storage (e.g., TPM).

Case: Samsung Galaxy S10 Fingerprint Bypass (2019) What Happened: 1 Galaxy S10 used an ultrasonic fingerprint sensor under the screen. With certain third-party screen protectors, any fingerprint could unlock the phone. The scanner misread patterns in the protector as valid fingerprints. Why This Is an Inherence-Based Authentication Flaw: 2 Relied on biometric (fingerprint) input — 'something you are'. Showed how biometric sensors can be spoofed or tricked. Consequences: 3 Security of biometric factor was bypassed. Samsung had to issue a software fix and warn users against using unsupported protectors. Lesson: 4 Biometrics offer convenience, but aren't immune to failure. Inherence-based methods require secure sensors and fallback safeguards. A close-up photograph of a Samsung Galaxy S10 smartphone. TOTP (Time-based One-Time Password) The diagram illustrates the TOTP generation process in two parallel paths, both resulting in the same passcode: 829 170 . Top Path (User's phone): A QR code labeled "Shared: OTP Secret Key, issuer, period" is scanned by a "User's phone" containing an "Authenticator App (Authy, Google Authenticator, etc.)". This app, combined with a clock icon representing time, produces a "Passcode" of 829 170 . The process is labeled "hashed, truncated". A green checkmark is placed below the resulting passcode. Bottom Path (Application Infrastructure): The same QR code is scanned by "Servers" (represented by server rack icons). These servers, combined with a clock icon representing time, also produce a "Passcode" of 829 170 . This process is also labeled "hashed, truncated". Both paths are enclosed in dashed-line boxes, and the identical passcode output demonstrates that both the user's device and the infrastructure have synchronized clocks and use the same shared secret. Diagram illustrating TOTP generation by both a user's phone and application infrastructure. • It is generated by an authenticator app (e.g., Google Authenticator, Microsoft Authenticator). • The passcode is based on a shared secret and current timestamp. • The device and the server must have synchronized clocks. • No internet connection is required after setup. • Used in two-factor authentication (2FA) to prove possession. Push-based Authentication graph LR; User[Login initiated by user] --> Server[Authentication server sends push notification]; Server --> Device[User approves or denies request]; Device --> Server; Server --> User; The diagram illustrates the Push-based Authentication process. It shows three main components: a user (represented by a computer icon), an authentication server (represented by a server rack icon), and a mobile device (represented by a smartphone icon). The process flow is as follows: 1. The user initiates a login. 2. The authentication server sends a push notification to the mobile device. 3. The user approves or denies the request on the mobile device. 4. The response is sent back to the server. 5. Finally, access is granted or blocked to the user. Diagram of the Push-based Authentication flow • Push authentication sends a login approval request to your mobile app. • You simply tap 'Approve' or 'Deny' on your device. • It requires real-time communication between the IAM system and your device. • Provides a smoother user experience compared to typing codes. • May include context like login location, device, or IP address. • Not supported natively in Keycloak; external services like Duo or Azure AD are used. Challenge-Response Authentication How It Works Used when the authenticator app requires the user to enter a code shown by the server. The server displays a numeric challenge (e.g., 849123). User Action User enters this challenge code into their authenticator app. Response Generation The app uses a shared secret to compute a one-time response. Authentication The server verifies this response to authenticate the user. This method is less common than TOTP but is useful for device pairing or extra security. sequenceDiagram

Passkeys : Enrollment Creating a passkey sequenceDiagram
 participant User
 participant Passkey_provider
 participant Browser
 participant Frontend
 participant Backend

 User->>Frontend: Initiate passkey creation
 Frontend->>Backend: Request credential data
 Backend-->>Frontend: Send user info, challenge, credential IDs, etc.
 Frontend->>Browser: navigator.credentials.create()
 Browser->>Passkey_provider: Generate passkey
 Passkey_provider-->>User: User verification
 User-->>Passkey_provider: Successful verification
 Passkey_provider->>Passkey_provider: Passkey creation
 Passkey_provider-->>Browser: Return public key
 Browser->>Frontend: Return public key credential
 Frontend->>Backend: Send public key credential
 Backend->>Backend: Store public key and data
 Backend-->>User: Send notification The diagram illustrates the passkey enrollment process across five entities: User, Passkey provider, Browser, Frontend, and Backend. The process begins with the User initiating passkey creation, which is received by the Frontend. The Frontend then requests credential data from the Backend, which responds with user info, challenges, and credential IDs. The Frontend uses this to initiate navigator.credentials.create() in the Browser. The Browser generates a passkey and sends it to the Passkey provider for user verification. Upon successful verification, the Passkey provider creates the passkey and returns the public key to the Browser. The Browser then returns a public key credential to the Frontend, which sends it to the Backend. The Backend stores the public key and data, and finally sends a notification back to the User. The diagram also indicates that the initial steps (User to Frontend) are part of the CATP (Credential Authentication and Transfer Protocol) and the subsequent steps (Frontend to Backend) are part of the WebAuthn (Web Authentication) standard. Sequence diagram showing the passkey enrollment process between User, Passkey provider, Browser, Frontend, and Backend. Passkeys : Sign in Creating a passkey sequenceDiagram
 participant User
 participant PP as Passkey provider
 participant B as Browser
 participant F as Frontend
 participant BE as Backend

 User->>F: Visits sign-in page
 F->>BE: Request auth challenge
 BE-->>F: Respond with challenge
 F->>B: navigator.credentials.get()
 B->>PP: Show autofill passkey dialog
 PP-->>User: User verification
 User-->>PP: Successful verification
 PP-->>B: Return public key with signature
 B->>F: Resolve promise with credential (signature)
 F->>BE: Send public key credential (signature)
 BE->>BE: Verify against stored public key
 BE-->>F: Authentication success
 F-->>User: Sign-in success The diagram illustrates the sign-in process for passkeys. It involves five main components: User, Passkey provider, Browser, Frontend, and Backend. The process begins with the User visiting the sign-in page on the Frontend. The Frontend then requests an authentication challenge from the Backend. The Backend responds with the challenge, which the Frontend passes to the Browser via navigator.credentials.get() . The Browser shows an autofill passkey dialog to the User for verification. Upon successful verification, the Passkey provider returns a public key and a signature to the Browser. The Browser then resolves this promise and sends the credential (signature) to the Frontend. The Frontend sends the public key credential (signature) to the Backend, which verifies it against the stored public key. Once authentication is successful, the Frontend informs the User of sign-in success. Sequence diagram showing the sign-in process for passkeys involving User, Passkey provider, Browser, Frontend, and Backend. From Method to Protocol: Why Protocols Matter Methods & Protocols Authentication methods = how users prove who they are (e.g., password, Face ID, smartcard). Authentication protocols = how systems communicate and validate that proof securely. 🧠 Analogy: 'Methods' are like saying your name; 'protocols' are the secure mail that delivers it to someone who needs to verify it. The Delivery Chain Think of protocols as the delivery mechanism that moves credentials between: • Your browser or app • An identity provider (like Google or Azure AD) • The system you're trying to access

They are set against a background of glowing circuit lines and data points. Why Authentication Protocols Matter ✓ Authentication protocols solve critical problems in digital identity: 1. Secure exchange of authentication data - Prevent replay or man-in-the-middle attacks 2. Interoperability across platforms and systems - Use Google login on a third-party app 3. Support federation (IDP ≠ Application) - Authenticate once, access multiple services 4. Enable method reuse (e.g., biometrics via FIDO2) - Consistent login across devices and channels 💡 Without protocols, authentication stays local and non-portable.

Protocol Matching 1 VPN login → RADIUS - RADIUS is commonly used to authenticate remote access through VPNs. 2 Wi-Fi at school → Kerberos - Many school networks use Active Directory for authentication, which relies on Kerberos internally. - Especially relevant for domain-joined devices on Windows networks. 3 Google login on Trello → OIDC - This uses OpenID Connect for federated web login, authenticating via a third-party identity provider. Tip: Think about the environment — web, enterprise, or infrastructure — to match the right protocol.

SAML & OIDC as Authentication Protocols SAML and OIDC are protocols used to delegate authentication to a trusted Identity Provider (IdP). ✓ Purpose: • Allow users to log in once and access multiple applications (SSO). • Transfer identity information from IdP to applications. 🔄 Authentication Perspective: • User logs in at the Identity Provider. • IdP sends proof of identity to the application (e.g., via token or assertion). • The app trusts the IdP to verify the user. 1 We'll explore federation setups and deep-dive into these protocols in Session 5. SAML & OIDC as Authentication Protocols The diagram illustrates the SAML & OIDC authentication flow involving four main components: End User, Application (Client), Resource Provider (Relying Party), and Authorization Server. The flow is as follows: ① Authentication Request : The Application (Client) sends an authentication request to the Authorization Server. ② Access Token and ID Token : The Authorization Server returns the Access Token and ID Token to the Application (Client). ③ Resource Call : The Application (Client) calls the Resource Provider (Relying Party). ④ Access Token Validation : The Resource Provider (Relying Party) validates the Access Token with the Authorization Server. ⑤ Resource Response : The Resource Provider (Relying Party) returns the resource response to the Application (Client).
